slides.title: One tool. Four providers.
slides.notes: DriveTest Analyzer is no longer a tool for NetCheck CDRs only. This deck covers the multi-provider model (NetCheck today, then Umlaut, P3 and RootMetrics), the time plan of their adaptation, how the tool is built inside, how it runs on AWS today and how it could run in the Ericsson cloud, and what we need to finish.

slides.title: A complete platform, built for NetCheck
slides.notes: Today the tool is complete, but everything is written in NetCheck names and values: ingestion, the Scoring formulas, the PPT templates, the NQ definition and the radio tables of Network Insights. The figures come from the repository at version 0.12.2 (10 main modules, 146k lines of Python, 100k of web interface, 2,386 automated tests in 154 files) and the UK workspace.

slides.title: Four providers, four languages
slides.notes: Each provider delivers its CDRs differently. NetCheck groups them by CDR type and operator; Umlaut splits them by service and by side of the call, and adds its own Qualifier. We have no P3 or RootMetrics sample yet; the Umlaut files themselves link to a P3 path, which suggests the formats may be related. RootMetrics comes in after P3, with the same model.

slides.title: One workspace, one provider.
slides.notes: Decision made: the CDRs of different providers are never mixed in one workspace. Every module therefore works with a single vocabulary, one Scoring methodology and one set of templates, and people who know Umlaut recognise its fields and files.

slides.title: Five rules of the multi-provider model
slides.notes: The five agreed rules: one provider per workspace, native names visible, Scoring with each provider’s own methodology, each provider’s NQ definition, and the DT Analyzer RCA as the common engine, available in every workspace and shown first, beside the provider’s RCA and the Ericsson RCA.

slides.title: Three layers per provider
slides.notes: The reader understands the structure of each provider’s export. The profile tells every module where each piece of data is and how to read it. The content is the provider’s own methodologies, templates and rules. The modules are not duplicated: the same logic serves every provider, from Scoring & GAP Analysis to the AI Assistant.

slides.title: One concept, each provider’s name
slides.notes: The profile is the central piece. For each provider, every concept a module needs has its native column, its conversion (for example kbit/s to Mbit/s) and the meaning of its values (SUCCESS stands for Completed). The Umlaut call setup is measured up to the alerting by default; the CDR Field Dictionary of Workspace Config can change it to Option D, as any other field. Users keep seeing the native column; the module reads the concept. The 84 of 109 figure comes from the compatibility analysis.

slides.title: What each provider changes in each module
slides.notes: Builders work as soon as the CDR can be loaded. CDR Analysis, Reporting and the AI Assistant barely change, because they reuse the calculations of the other modules. The Workspace already has the Umlaut reader and upload (phase 2). Scoring & GAP Analysis, PPT Designer and Non-Qualified Calls need the content of each provider, and the Layer3 Logs a pre-processing script per provider. The major change is Network Insights, because Umlaut only gives the radio of a call at its start and end and has no identity for NR cells. Ticket Center does not read CDRs.

slides.title: One RCA of our own for every provider
slides.notes: The DT Analyzer RCA is available in every workspace and shows first among the RCA sources. It reads each call through the profile of its provider: its result and failure, the LTE and NR radio of both sides, its mobility and KPIs, and the network around it from the Network Inventory; ordered rules that each workspace can edit give the root category and cause, with the evidence. What each provider still needs are its values and its failure catalogue. The rules shown are examples of the kind of condition, not a closed catalogue.

slides.title: From the base to RootMetrics, in eight phases
slides.notes: Phases 1 and 2 are done in version 0.9.0, and the Umlaut CDRs were checked with the columnar copy in 0.11.0. Phases 3 to 6 bring Umlaut to Scoring, PPT Designer, Non-Qualified Calls with the RCA and Layer3 inputs, and Network Insights; the DT Analyzer RCA and the NR cells found by PCI and ARFCN already exist. P3 and then RootMetrics come next with the same model, as soon as there is a sample of each. The dates follow the time plan of the next slide.

slides.title: Umlaut, then P3, then RootMetrics
slides.notes: A plan of about eight to ten weeks per provider, one provider at a time. Umlaut needs nine weeks from January 2027 (Scoring 3, PPT templates 1, Non-Qualified Calls with the RCA and Layer3 2, Network Insights 2, and 1 of validation with the teams), so Umlaut CDR would be supported in March 2027. P3 follows in ten weeks with its compatibility report, reader and profile, its Scoring and its content, supported in May 2027; RootMetrics follows in the same way, supported in July 2027. Each provider starts only once its inputs are in, and a later input moves its bars by the same time; the Christmas weeks are left out.

slides.title: The multi-provider base, NetCheck untouched
slides.notes: Phase 1 prepares the tool without changing anything for NetCheck users. The modules no longer hold NetCheck names inside; they ask the workspace’s profile for them. The NetCheck profile reproduces exactly the previous columns, and the validation proved it: processing the same real NetCheck CDRs before and after the change gave 89 of 89 identical outputs, and every related test passes. RootMetrics CDR was added beside them as coming soon in 0.12.2.

slides.title: From columns inside each module to one profile
slides.notes: Before phase 1, each module carried its own lists of NetCheck column names. Now they all live in one field profile per CDR type, in cdr_field_profiles.py, and every module asks for the profile of its workspace. For NetCheck the profile holds exactly the previous columns, so the same CDRs give the same results: 89 of 89 outputs were identical on a real sample of the UK workspace. A workspace with CDRs can no longer change its CDR type, and Umlaut, P3 and RootMetrics appear as coming soon.

slides.title: What changed in the code
slides.notes: File by file: a new module with the profiles; the CDR type registry with P3 and the lock; and the modules that read CDR columns, which now take them from the workspace’s profile instead of their own NetCheck lists. The app passes the profile when it processes a CDR. There is no database migration, so restarting the application changes nothing in existing workspaces. The second commit only updates two NQ tests that already failed before phase 1.

slides.title: Umlaut CDRs read with their own names
slides.notes: Phase 2 reads Umlaut CDRs with their own names. The Umlaut reader takes every service workbook as a CDR, ignores the Statistics sheet, reads one operator per client sheet and keeps the headers of the second side of a call apart; All_Data and All_Voice are summaries, not CDRs. The Umlaut profile keeps the native names, reads SUCCESS, FAILED and DROPPED as Completed, Failed and Dropped, converts kbit/s to Mbit/s and measures call setup up to Alerting by default (Option D through the dictionary). Derived columns add the Campaign from the benchmark of the file name, a Test_Key for the data tests and the ECI of the serving cell. On upload each file takes its type from its service name, as a Final CDR. In Non-Qualified Calls a call or test is NQ when its qualifier says NOT QUALIFIED, with the DT Analyzer RCA. The CDR Field Dictionary of Workspace Config shows and edits the 211 fields per workspace. Umlaut CDR stays coming soon until a multi-operator export validates it.

slides.title: A real Umlaut export, NetCheck untouched
slides.notes: Phase 2 was validated in three ways. The same real NetCheck CDRs give exactly the same results before and after the change (90 of 90 outputs). The automated tests pass (894). And the real WindTre Round 1 Umlaut export was processed in a test workspace: 478 NQ (52 Voice calls, 26 Speech calls with 285 samples, 3 File DL and 397 Interactivity tests), classified by the DT Analyzer RCA. Ping and DNS have no qualifier, so they have no NQ. Since 0.11.0 the same export is read identically from its columnar copy in every module (13 CDRs, 194,053 rows), guarded by tests.

slides.title: How the tool is built
slides.notes: A single FastAPI application on Python 3.15 serves the web interface (Jinja2 templates and JavaScript) and the API. Each module is a Python package that reads the CDRs from their Parquet copies with DuckDB; SQLite keeps the configuration, the follow-up and the results of each workspace. Heavy work, such as processing a CDR or generating a report, runs in the background: a scheduler with priorities per workspace and isolated workers, so the interface stays responsive. Exports use python-pptx and python-docx, LibreOffice for previews and Chromium with Node.js to draw the charts; the AI engine (Kiro CLI or Claude) writes slide comments and answers in the AI Assistant, with the names sent as codes.

slides.title: From the uploaded file to the report
slides.notes: This is how the tool walks a CDR. It is uploaded and its type, NR Mode and stage are confirmed. The provider’s reader decides what is CDR. The profile fills the internal layer the modules use. Then the mappings are applied and the CDR is copied to its Parquet files, read with DuckDB, and its table is emptied. A later change rewrites only the columns that change in the copy, never putting the rows back in SQLite.

slides.title: Every workspace is self-contained
slides.notes: Global configuration lives in APP_CONFIG_DIR and everything that belongs to a workspace in its own folder under APP_DATA_DIR: its database (settings, NQ follow-up, Scoring and App Events), the Parquet copy of every CDR in .cdr-store, the uploaded files, the generated output and the caches. The columnar copy made Network Insights 79 times faster and the workspace database 10 times lighter, and Tableau reads the same copies. A workspace can be transferred to another server or restored on its own, and its CDR type travels with it.

slides.title: One container with everything inside
slides.notes: The production image is built by GitHub Actions on every push and published on Docker Hub for AMD64 and ARM64, with a latest-noavx variant for CPUs without AVX2: python:3.15-slim with the Python packages (FastAPI, pandas, GeoPandas, DuckDB, python-pptx…), the tools the exports need (Chromium and Node.js to draw charts, LibreOffice for previews), the Help presentations generator and the application code, stamped with its Git revision. Compose publishes port 7278, checks /healthz every 30 seconds, restarts the container unless it is stopped and mounts the config and data volumes, where all state lives; HTTPS is served in front of it.

slides.title: Deployment on AWS
slides.notes: The architecture as it runs today, in the account of the team in eu-west-1: the AWS Cloud, the Region and the VPC with its public subnet hold the EC2 instance inside its security group. Everything comes in through the Internet gateway, the IN gate: the users over HTTPS on 8443, which Caddy serves with a Let’s Encrypt certificate and passes to the tool on 7278, and Tableau over PostgreSQL with TLS on 5432, to the tableau-db container (PostgreSQL 17 with pg_duckdb, refreshed every 5 minutes by a systemd timer); there is no SSH from the internet, only from the internal network. Administrators sign in with AWS SSO and open a Session Manager session: the SSM Agent of the instance connects out, so no port is opened for them. Everything goes out through the same Internet gateway over HTTPS, the OUT gate: Dockhand pulls each new image from Docker Hub, built by GitHub Actions, and recreates the tool; the tool reaches the Power Automate flow of the emails, the AI engine, OpenStreetMap and the other servers of the tool. Two EBS volumes are attached: a 50 GB root for the system and the Docker images, pruned every week, and a 1 TiB /data volume with the config, the workspaces, the backups and the Tableau database. There is no load balancer, VPN, ECR, Secrets Manager or SES; snapshots of /data are recommended.

slides.title: Deployment in the Ericsson cloud
slides.notes: A proposal for the Ericsson cloud, drawn like the AWS architecture and with the same image and volumes. The VM sits in a private subnet with no public IP, inside a virtual network of the project. The way in is the corporate firewall: the teams reach the tool over HTTPS on 443 from the Ericsson network, served by Caddy with a corporate certificate and a DNS name, and Tableau Server reaches tableau-db over TLS on 5432; nothing is open to the internet. Administrators go through the jump host, the only source allowed for SSH on 22. The way out is the corporate proxy, over HTTPS: Dockhand pulls the image from Docker Hub or an internal mirror, and the tool reaches the Power Automate flow of the emails, the AI engine if the policy allows it, OpenStreetMap and the AWS server, for transfers both ways. A 50 GB system disk and a 1 TB block volume with the config, the workspaces, the backups and the Tableau database, with snapshots of the platform.

slides.title: Running it day to day
slides.notes: Operating the tool needs little: scheduled light backups between weekly full ones, kept by days, weeks and months below the data volume; upgrades by pulling the image built on every push and recreating the container, with database migrations at startup; the /healthz endpoint for the platform and App Logs and App Events for traceability; and transfers, offers and requests, to move workspaces and content between servers. Snapshots of the data volume by the platform are still recommended.

slides.title: From one server to the cloud at scale
slides.notes: Today the tool scales up: one container per server, the background work inside it and SQLite for configuration, follow-up and results. Versions 0.10 to 0.12 moved the CDR rows to Parquet read with DuckDB, which replaced the move to PostgreSQL planned before (Network Insights 79 times faster, the Points Lost Map more than 300 times), and connected Tableau through PostgreSQL with pg_duckdb. Next on the roadmap: health monitoring with alerts on runs that take too long, automated end-to-end deployment checks, and more providers on the same model.

slides.title: What we need to continue
slides.notes: To complete Umlaut, P3 and RootMetrics we need, for each of them: CDR exports of a real benchmark (for Umlaut a multi-operator one, ideally with NR SA and walk or train tests, which also validates its reader so that Umlaut CDR stops being coming soon); a description of the P3 and RootMetrics formats; the Scoring methodology documents of each provider (KPIs, thresholds, weights, categories and areas, with a published scoring to check ours against), without which Scoring & GAP Analysis cannot be built; a pre-processing script of the Layer3 logs of each provider that keeps only the NQ calls and the columns needed, by the call key of the provider, as we have for NetCheck, whose output is the Layer3 Logs we upload; the Network Inventories of each country; the failure catalogue of each provider; the Ericsson RCA keyed by the call key of each provider; and the PowerPoint reports the teams deliver today.

slides.title: The Network Inventories we need
slides.notes: The Network Inventories we need for the country of each benchmark, for every operator in it: the LTE cells with their identity (eNodeB ID and Cell ID, or ECI), PCI, EARFCN, band, bandwidth, TAC, site, cell name, position and azimuth; the NR cells with the gNodeB ID, its length and the Cell ID (or NCI), PCI, SSB NR-ARFCN, band, bandwidth, NSA or SA, position and azimuth, which let the tool find the NR cells by PCI, ARFCN and distance where the CDR has no NCI, as in Umlaut; for each cell, the network that owns it, the Host Network whose RAN carries it, its Vendor, its status, height and tilts; one snapshot per campaign, in CSV, Excel or Cell Configuration KMZ; and the Region and Cluster polygons of the performance owners, with Vendor polygons where there is no inventory. A Multivendor Mapping can give the Vendor when the inventory has none.
